sm: The host, Jeremy Boreing, opens with a monologue on the midterms. He says Democrats took the House and the Senate, flipped seven Republican Senate seats including Kansas, and won both the Senate seat and the governorship in Texas. He notes the president said he was not on the ballot, even though he had urged Republicans to pretend he was, and cites polling that more voters wanted to oppose him than support him. He argues Trump has few lasting legislative wins, relied on executive action, and let his tariffs, the Iran strikes and the stalled war hurt the economy and gas prices. He says about two thirds of voters felt the tariffs hurt the economy.

Boreing continues by raising questions about Trump family business deals, including a reported half billion dollar crypto purchase by people tied to an Abu Dhabi royal. He says more voters named corruption as crucial to their vote than the cost of living, and he thinks 2028 looks very hard for Republicans. He blames loud voices on the right, such as Nick Fuentes, Tucker Carlson and others, for a demoralization campaign that urged people to stay home. He notes that white evangelical share of the electorate fell and that men under thirty swung toward Democrats. He closes by urging people not to despair, to put faith in God, and to get back to work.

Boreing ends his opening by saying the day of defeat is what the movement is for, and that pessimism is a self-fulfilling prophecy. He introduces his guests: Matthias Shapiro, a software engineer and data analyst, Eric Erickson, the talk radio host, and Dr. Owen Strachan, a theologian and author. Erickson says exit polls show voters support capitalism, free trade and smaller government, so Republicans can recover if they return to those principles. Shapiro points to Florida, where Ron DeSantis built a resilient party, and says Republicans need a farm team. The group then notes the rise of liberal Protestantism in Texas and Kansas, and Boreing says young men are drifting toward older traditions like Catholicism and Orthodoxy.

The guests discuss the risk that evangelicalism could be left mostly to women if young men leave, and how a sincere liberal Protestant like Texas's Talarico could pull young people. They describe two opposite problems: a leftist, TikTok-style religion on campuses, and an identitarian, blood-and-soil mood among young white men who have turned against Israel and the American idea. Erickson says people replace God with government and power, and that churches should offer belonging without becoming political. Strachan says evangelicals have failed to make a case for masculine strength. They also criticize parts of the right, and the vice president at times, for telling young men they are victims.

The conversation turns to young men and the right's failures toward them, including telling them they have no problems or blaming them. Erickson praises the Jordan Peterson message of cleaning up your room and describes churches pairing young men with older men. They say fighting-age young men can become destructive if not marshaled, and that some new-right voices want to point them against the American experiment. They discuss how the woke left took American history, and now parts of the right do the same, citing Darryl Cooper on Churchill. They also discuss the Anakin Skywalker meme among Gen Z men, which Erickson says surfaced through anonymous accounts, and note that online and real life are merging.

The guests discuss how Gen Z may have a pagan rather than Christian foundation, and how young people have lost shared history and the Western canon. Boreing argues people learn more from culture and entertainment than from formal education, and that evangelicals get their theology from songs more than sermons. They name Charlie Kirk and Jordan Peterson as lost good influences on young men. Erickson says the loss was also about Trump, with Republicans wiped out in Georgia and Texas. He says young men felt betrayed because Trump promised to fight for them but fought for a ballroom, a golf course and enriching his family, and Republicans would not correct him.

Erickson continues, citing the shooting of Alex Pretti as a protester during a deportation raid and Hispanic men who now feel they must carry proof of citizenship. The guests compare the result to the 1974 post-Watergate midterms, and say people feel betrayed at a personal level, not just routinely repudiating a president. They mention retirement accounts stagnating, high gas prices, and young graduates unable to find jobs. One guest warns that the new right will blame neoconservatives and call for more populism, while another says the president, not neocons, took the country into the Iran war. They argue the vice president's claim that the war lost the election leaves out that he structured the memorandum of understanding.

The guests argue that a country going to war has a moral duty to win, and that the Iran war lost support after the memorandum of understanding. They ask who will be fired over the war, the missile shortage, the Canada trade war and the tariffs. Boreing says Trump's appeal was that people felt he wanted America to win, and that failure makes people hate those associated with it, as with the Bushes. They credit Trump with fewer federal workers and negative net migration, but call these ephemeral wins that can be undone because nothing was done legislatively. They say George W. Bush secured more lasting legislative gains, even with Democrats controlling Congress.

The guests say governing through executive power creates instability that hurts businesses, and note the stock market rose that morning because of expected stability. Erickson tells of a home builder friend hurt by tariffs, and says the administration's own data shows seven to ten people hurt for every one helped. They say voters want a positive vision, and one guest is less pessimistic about 2028 than Boreing. They note a sitting vice president backed by the president has always won the nomination, but they are wary of JD Vance's stance on Israel and economic populism. They see an opening for a governor, and several say Ron DeSantis was the big winner of the night because he is not in the administration.

The guests praise DeSantis for his competence during COVID and wonder how to turn it into national appeal. Erickson, an election lawyer by background, says candidates who win primaries often lose general elections, pointing to Mike Collins in Georgia and Ken Paxton in Texas. The guests disagree about whether Republicans should vote for flawed nominees. Erickson and Boreing say general elections are team sports and primaries are the place to fix the problem, while others point to character fatigue and low Protestant turnout. Strachan says pastors face a real challenge urging votes for a candidate with a known mistress.

The guests explain that Paxton won the Texas nomination as the established attorney general, and that many of his wealthy donors abandoned him afterward. Erickson says John Cornyn should have been pressured not to run, and that leaders need someone to tell them when they have screwed up, advice he says came from Rush Limbaugh. They argue Cornyn would have done better in the general election, and that mid-decade redistricting and Trump loyalty pushed independents away. They reject the claim that Californians turned Texas blue, saying many are conservatives. They then turn to 2028: Rubio probably wants to make money, the history of the party favors Ted Cruz as the runner-up, and Cruz is tied to the administration through his Senate role.

Boreing, a Cruz supporter, asks if Cruz can run from the Senate amid coming investigations. The guests note his seat is not up until 2030, so he could stay as Texas's last man standing, or leave and let Governor Abbott name a successor. They debate whether he should defend the president or call out corruption as DeSantis did. Several praise Marco Rubio as a strong secretary of state who offers a hopeful vision and has avoided the new right's skepticism of Israel. They also say Rubio has moved toward economic populism. One guest says the next Republican nominee will either be a new-right figure or someone offering a positive, affirming vision.

The guests turn to the Democratic field, calling it the first real free-for-all since 2008. They list Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Kamala Harris, Pete Buttigieg, Josh Shapiro, Jon Ossoff, Gavin Newsom and Andy Beshear. They say South Carolina going first helps Harris and hurts Ocasio-Cortez. Boreing and the others call Ocasio-Cortez a generational political talent with great media instincts, pointing to her handling of a breakup video as an example. They think she would do well in debates against Cruz, Vance or Rubio, though they think Rubio would match her best as a relatable media figure.

The guests continue on 2028 candidates, with Erickson describing Jon Ossoff as robotic off teleprompter but very strong at constituent services for Georgia farmers. He says he did not vote in the Georgia Senate race because the Republican nominee was surrounded by antisemites and white nationalists. They discuss retail politics and the importance of image, referencing Roger Ailes's book You Are the Message. They then turn to antisemitism on the right. Strachan says older evangelicals are staunchly pro-Israel because of dispensationalism, but younger evangelicals have moved away from that theology, and many simply do not care about Israel.

Strachan says Tucker Carlson and Darryl Cooper are helping carry antisemitism into a Christian framework, and cites Joel Webb and others gaining traction with antisemitic edges. He notes a Christian conference in Utah that let a pro-Hitler publisher have a table. He cites John four twenty-two, that salvation is of the Jews, and says Christians cannot midwife antisemitism. Another guest says media telling Jewish stories like Schindler's List has faded, leaving young people without grounding. Boreing says reformed skeptics of Israel ironically fulfill dispensationalist expectations, argues Israel's existence is a clear sign of biblical significance, and rejects claims that modern Jews are not the real Jews.

Boreing describes attending a Shabbat service at the Songs of David Synagogue, where Psalms are sung in the hills where David tended sheep. He says this makes the claim that they are not the Jews absurd. The guests say some critics apply moral blame to Jews across all history while denying continuity when it suits them. Strachan says Christians should support Jews because of Paul in Romans eleven, not only eschatology, and wonders if God is gathering in the Jews while Christian nationalists oppose them. Erickson then asks where the parents are for radicalized young men, and Boreing defends them, saying divorce blows up the planet children live on.

Boreing explains that he cannot fully grasp what divorce does to a child, since he remembers life before his daughter and wife while they know no other. He says young men asking where the parents were are asking a fair question. The group then calls social media the most destructive force ever unleashed, even though it has benefited them, and says it makes even attentive parents' efforts harder. Erickson says the country has a spiritual crisis, not a political one, and that people look for political saviors for spiritual problems. He warns the church is bringing in too much politics and turning people off, quoting Chuck Colson that salvation does not come on Air Force One.

The guests say Americans seek political saviors for spiritual problems, and that figures like Joel Webb exploit it. Returning to Anakin Skywalker, they say he is fatherless and preyed on by a dark father in Palpatine, like fatherless young men drawn to the darker parts of the new right. Strachan suggests a simple strategy of discipling young men, with older men putting an arm around them in love at church. Boreing then tells a story about his seventh grade football coach, Greg Hernandez, who let him join the team despite knowing nothing about the sport. The coach made him a receiver and told him never to touch the football and to run to the goal post.

Boreing finishes the football story. He followed the coach's rules, ran hard every play and never touched the ball. In the last game of an undefeated season, a fumble rolled in front of him in the end zone, and he did not pick it up because he had promised. He did not know what an end zone was, and the team lost the chance to score. He says he would love to coach boys because of the influence Hernandez had on him, and that investing in young men is God's work, more important than any election. He says losing costs potential, but nothing matters more than how you live and invest in the fatherless who are tempted by the dark father, and thanks his guests.
